title: Tomb Guardians

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, Gift of various donors to the department of Asian Art (by exchange) (2000.118)
image.license: Public domain. Released under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access program

altText: A pair of tall standing figures made of glazed ceramic. One has the face of an animal with antlers, and the other has a human face with large ears, a short horn and flame-like hair.

context: A pair of glazed earthenware figures from China's Tang dynasty (618–907), made in the early 700s and probably from Xi'an. The Cleveland Museum of Art describes them as earth-spirit (qitou) tomb guardians, protective figures meant to guard a tomb entrance. The two parts are about 89 and 92 cm tall.

descriptions.k: Look at the two tall figures made of clay with shiny glaze. One has an animal face and one has a human face. Point to the big ears and the horns. What colors do you see?
descriptions.g12: These two tall figures were made in China long ago from clay with shiny glaze. They are protective guardians. One has an animal face with antlers. The other has a human face, big ears, a short horn and hair like flames. Which face do you look at first? Why?
descriptions.g35: This pair of tomb guardians was made in China in the early 700s, during the Tang dynasty. The makers used glazed earthenware in the three-color sancai style. One guardian has an animal face with antlers, and the other has a human face with large ears, a short horn and fiery hair. Compare the two figures. How do their faces and poses make them look protective?
descriptions.g68: These Tang dynasty tomb guardians (early 700s) are earth-spirit figures, or qitou, meant to guard a tomb entrance. The museum notes they were carried in funerary processions before being placed in tombs. They are glazed earthenware in sancai, or three-color, ware. One has an animal face with antlers and the other a human face with a short horn. How do the features and colors show their protective role?
descriptions.g910: Made in the early 700s, these Tang dynasty earth-spirit guardians (qitou) were carried in funerary processions and placed to protect a tomb entrance. The sancai glazes include costly cobalt blue, which the museum links to the high status of the tomb's occupant. One face is an animal's with antlers and one is human with a short horn and fiery hair. How do materials and imagery work together to communicate protection and status?
descriptions.g1112: These paired guardians from Tang China (early 700s), probably made near Xi'an, were carried in funerary processions and placed to guard a tomb entrance. The sancai glazes and imported cobalt blue point to the status of the tomb's occupant. The animal-faced and human-faced figures combine ferocity with order. How does the pairing of different faces shape the meaning of the work, and what does imported cobalt suggest about the Tang world?

g12.observation: Describe the horn, ears and hair on the human-faced guardian.

g35.shape: What forms do you see in the bodies and heads, and how do they make the figures look sturdy?
g35.color: The museum says cobalt blue was costly. How does the blue stand out among the sancai colors?
g35.texture: How do you think the glazed surface differs from an unglazed clay surface?
g35.space: How are the figures made to feel large and powerful even though they are under one meter tall?
g35.light: How might light bring out the shine of the glaze and the shape of the faces?
g35.meaning: The guardians were meant to ward off evil. What features might help scare it away?
g35.culture: What do the sancai glazes and cobalt blue suggest about the person for whom these were made?
g35.technique: Why do you think the makers chose earthenware and glaze for these guardians?

g68.daily: How do the contrasting faces, one animal and one human, create a sense of range in the pair's protective power?
g68.emotion: How do the intense expressions and bold glaze colors shape the mood of the pair?
g68.observation: Compare the details above the eyebrows and on the head of each guardian. What differences do you see?
g68.analysis: How does the paired composition create balance while still allowing each guardian its own character?
g68.line: How do the swept lines of hair, antlers and horn create a sense of energy?
g68.shape: How do the solid, upright forms of the bodies support their role as guardians?
g68.color: The museum says the cobalt blue on the human-faced guardian was imported from the Middle East. What might that suggest about trade?
g68.texture: How does glazing change the surface compared with painted or bare earthenware?
g68.space: How do the heights of about 89 and 92 cm affect the way viewers would meet these figures?
g68.light: How might shine on glazed surfaces have changed the way the figures were seen in a procession?
g68.meaning: How can fierce faces serve both to threaten evil spirits and to comfort the living?
g68.culture: How do these figures reflect Tang ideas about death, protection and respect for the deceased?
g68.technique: What does the sancai technique show about the skills of Tang potters and workshops?
g68.personal: What would a modern protective object look like, and what features would it share with these guardians?
g68.critical: How do you decide how to describe a funerary object respectfully when you read it as art?

g910.daily: How do the divergent faces of the animal-headed and human-headed guardians build a layered image of protection?
g910.emotion: What tone do the fierce features and strong colors establish for those who encountered the figures at the tomb entrance?
g910.observation: Examine the handling of the antlers, the short horn and the fiery hair. What do they reveal about the makers' attention to the guardians' spiritual character?
g910.analysis: How does the paired arrangement use difference as a compositional strategy?
g910.line: How do the rhythmic, flame-like forms organize the upper parts of the figures?
g910.shape: How do the compact, upright bodies communicate stability while the heads and hair suggest motion?
g910.color: What does the use of imported cobalt blue suggest about the economic and cultural connections of Tang China?
g910.texture: How does sancai glazing turn earthenware into a luxury surface, and what does that imply about its owner?
g910.space: How does the scale of the figures, close to human size, affect the viewer's encounter with them in a funerary context?
g910.light: How might lustrous glaze have shaped the figures' appearance in torchlight or daylight during the procession?
g910.meaning: How can an object made for a funeral serve both the living, as part of a public rite, and the dead, as a guardian?
g910.culture: How does the museum's note that the glazes suggest the tomb occupant's high status shape our reading of the figures as social markers?
g910.technique: What can the glaze palette tell us about technical knowledge and workshop organization in Tang China?
g910.personal: How does your own cultural background shape the way you read protective figures made for a different tradition?
g910.critical: What are the limits of describing these figures through today's categories of art, and how can a viewer avoid imposing them?

g1112.daily: How does the pairing of animal-faced and human-faced guardians construct a hybrid, multilayered idea of protection?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the figures' fierce features and imported blue glaze have shaped the emotional register of a funerary procession?
g1112.observation: Scan the details of antlers, horn, ears and flame-like hair. What do they reveal about the iconography of earth-spirit guardians?
g1112.analysis: How does the diptych-like pairing balance symmetry and difference, and what interpretive work does that balance do?
g1112.line: How do the sweeping, flame-like forms produce a dynamic silhouette against the figures' stable bodies?
g1112.shape: How do the figures reconcile monumentality of posture with the fluid forms of hair and ornament?
g1112.color: What does the presence of cobalt blue, which the museum says was imported from the Middle East, suggest about Tang China's place in long-distance exchange?
g1112.texture: How does the combination of earthenware body and polychrome glaze convey wealth, and how might glaze have signaled rank to mourners?
g1112.space: How does the figures' near-human scale shape their function as presences at a tomb entrance?
g1112.light: How might the glaze's reflective surface have contributed to the figures' ceremonial effect in procession and in the tomb?
g1112.meaning: How does a work designed to be carried in a funeral procession and then buried complicate the idea of art as something for display?
g1112.culture: How might the museum's observation about status complicate the idea that guardians are about spiritual protection alone?
g1112.technique: What does sancai production suggest about the scale and sophistication of Tang ceramic workshops?
g1112.personal: How do your own assumptions about death and ritual shape how you approach these figures, and how can you check them against the evidence?
g1112.critical: What cautions are needed in interpreting individual features, like the horn or the fiery hair, when the evidence we have is limited to the objects and a museum's account?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Metadata-screened from the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access API record (title, culture, date, medium, creditline, description, did_you_know, CC0 status). Sensitive aspect for the reviewer: these are funerary objects (tomb guardians) with fierce faces; no human remains, nudity or violence are indicated. They are described factually as protective figures of the Tang dynasty and K-3 text keeps to shapes, colors and materials, with the funerary role stated in older bands. The record is the parent object 2000.118 (a pair); the separate parts 2000.118.1 (animal head with antlers) and 2000.118.2 (human face) also exist. The record gives no named artist, so the artist field is 'Unidentified makers'. The image file has not been viewed; a person should confirm it before release.

teacherNote.context: A pair of glazed earthenware earth-spirit (qitou) tomb guardians in sancai (three-color) ware from Tang dynasty China (618–907), made in the early 700s and probably from the Xi'an area. The Cleveland Museum of Art says they were meant to guard a tomb entrance and were carried in funerary processions before being placed in tombs.
directions: Ask younger students to compare the two faces and describe the colors, ears, horns and hair they see.
Have students design a guardian figure for a place they care about, choosing the face, colors and materials.
Ask older students to discuss why a culture would make guardian figures for a tomb and what the materials suggest about the person buried there.
